title: Three Cup Chicken
subtitle: Taiwanese chicken braised in sesame oil, soy sauce and rice wine with fresh basil
excerpt: Three cup chicken is a Taiwanese classic named for its three equal measures of sesame oil, soy sauce and rice wine. Bone-in chicken pieces are fried in sesame oil with garlic and ginger, braised until the sauce reduces to a dark, sticky glaze, then finished with a large handful of fresh basil. Serves 4 in about 35 minutes.
sourceNotes: Three cup chicken, known in Mandarin as san bei ji, is one of the most iconic dishes of Taiwanese home cooking, though it has roots in Jiangxi province in mainland China. The dish and its history are discussed in Cathy Erway's 'The Food of Taiwan' (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015), which traces the recipe's spread through Taiwan during the twentieth century and notes that the original equal-measure formula is now widely adjusted for modern tastes, with less oil and more wine than the traditional version.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Taiwanese cooking method in which equal volumes of sesame oil, soy sauce and rice wine are used as the base for a braise. The three liquids reduce together into a concentrated, glossy sauce. Modern versions often use more rice wine and less sesame oil than the original formula, as sesame oil can become overpowering in large quantities.

Oil pressed from toasted sesame seeds, dark amber in colour and strongly flavoured. It is used as a finishing oil and flavouring rather than a cooking oil in most applications, but in three cup chicken it is used as the primary cooking fat from the start, which gives the dish its distinctive rich, nutty base.

A variety of Asian basil with slightly smaller leaves and a stronger, more anise-like flavour than Italian basil. It is also sold as Thai basil. It is added to three cup chicken at the very end of cooking so the heat wilts it but does not destroy its fragrance. Regular basil is a poor substitute; use Thai basil if Taiwanese basil is unavailable.

A Chinese fermented rice wine named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. It has a rich, slightly nutty flavour and is the standard rice wine used in Chinese cooking, though in Taiwan a local michiu (rice wine) is traditional for three cup chicken. Shaoxing wine works very well.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 35 minutes. The

is simple: the three liquids go in together and reduce to a thick, concentrated sauce while the chicken finishes cooking. The key is to not walk away once the sauce starts reducing, as it can catch and burn at the end.
Bone-in chicken gives far more flavour than boneless here, as the bones flavour the sauce during braising. Chicken thighs and drumsticks work best. The
goes in at the very end, off the heat or on very low, just long enough to wilt. Its fragrance is the final note of the dish.
Heat the {{sesame-oil}} in a wok or wide, heavy pan over a medium heat. Add the {{garlic}}, {{ginger}} and dried chillies if using. Fry for 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant and lightly golden.
Increase the heat to medium-high. Add the {{chicken-thighs}} skin-side down and fry for 4 to 5 minutes until the skin is well browned. Turn and brown the other side for 3 minutes.
Pour in the {{soy-sauce}}, {{shaoxing-wine}} and {{sugar}}. Stir to combine and bring to a simmer.

Cover and cook over a medium-low heat for 15 minutes, turning the chicken occasionally. Remove the lid and increase the heat to medium-high. Cook for a further 5 minutes, stirring and turning the chicken as the sauce reduces to a thick, glossy glaze that coats each piece.
Remove the pan from the heat. Add the {{thai-basil}} and toss quickly. The residual heat will wilt the leaves within 30 seconds. Serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.symptom: The sauce is burning on the bottom of the pan
items.cause: The heat is too high during the reduction or there is too little liquid
items.fix: Watch the pan closely once the lid comes off. Stir frequently and reduce the heat if the sauce is reducing faster than the chicken is cooking.

items.cause: The soy sauce brand is very salty or the ratio was not adjusted
items.fix: Use a light soy sauce rather than dark, and taste before adding any extra soy at the table. A little extra rice wine can dilute the saltiness.

items.symptom: The basil has gone black and bitter
items.cause: It was added while the pan was still on high heat
items.fix: Take the pan completely off the heat before adding the basil. The residual heat is sufficient to wilt the leaves without cooking them past their point.

content.text: Three cup chicken is one of Taiwan's best-known home-cooked dishes. It is served in night market stalls, simple restaurants and family kitchens across the island, and is one of the dishes most closely associated with Taiwanese rather than mainland Chinese cooking. The
used from the very beginning distinguishes it from most Chinese braised chicken dishes and gives it a richer, nuttier base than a Cantonese or Shanghainese equivalent. The
adds depth, and the basil at the end is what makes the dish distinctively Taiwanese.
